title: Concurrency: async/await, event loop, threads, processes and GIL
summary: async/await gives cooperative concurrency on a single thread with an event loop (asyncio), ideal for I/O waits.

sections.definition: async/await gives cooperative concurrency on a single thread with an event loop (asyncio): ideal for I/O waits. Threads are managed by the operating system, but in CPython the GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time: they help with I/O, they don't speed up computation. Processes give real parallelism for CPU work. Python 3.13+ offers an optional build without the GIL (free-threaded), but the standard installation still has it.
sections.analogy: The event loop is a waiter serving several tables: he takes an order and, while the kitchen prepares it (await), serves another table. Threads are several waiters sharing a single notepad (the GIL): only one writes at a time. Processes are several independent kitchens.
sections.problem: A time.sleep() or a blocking library inside a coroutine freezes the whole event loop: no other task makes progress.
sections.code:example:
import asyncio

async def consultar_inventario(producto: str) -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(1)        # simula I/O: BD, API externa
    return 10

async def main():
    resultados = await asyncio.gather(
        consultar_inventario("cafe"),
        consultar_inventario("taza"),
        consultar_inventario("filtro"),
    )                              # ~1 s en total, no 3 s
    print(resultados)              # [10, 10, 10]

asyncio.run(main())

# Código bloqueante dentro de async: mándalo a un hilo
resultado = await asyncio.to_thread(generar_pdf_factura, pedido_id)
sections.bad:
async def consultar(producto):
    time.sleep(1)                 # bloquea el loop
    return requests.get(url).json()  # requests es bloqueante

It looks async, but it handles one thing at a time.
sections.good:
async def consultar(producto):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.get(url)
    return r.json()

Every wait yields control to the event loop.
sections.bridge:typescript: The syntax is almost the same as JS and asyncio.gather ≈ Promise.all. Key difference: in JS a Promise starts running as soon as it is created; in Python a coroutine does nothing until you await it or turn it into a Task. Node also has a single thread with an event loop, but it has no GIL because it never had JS threads sharing memory. In JS you cancel with AbortController; asyncio has cancellable Tasks and async generators.
sections.interview: Async is concurrency on a single thread: the event loop switches between tasks every time one awaits on I/O, so it works for many network or database waits. Threads also work for I/O, but because of the GIL only one runs Python at a time, so they don't speed up computation. For CPU work I use processes. In FastAPI the important thing is not to block the event loop inside an async endpoint.
sections.myths:
• Calling an async function without await: you get a coroutine object and the "was never awaited" warning.
  • Using blocking libraries (requests, psycopg2, time.sleep) inside async def.
  • Believing async speeds up CPU computation: it only helps you wait better.
  • Using threads to parallelize heavy computation: the GIL serializes it.

exercises.prompt: Which concurrency tool would you use?

items.why: Many network waits with an async library.
Heavy CPU: the GIL blocks threads.

items.text: Using a blocking legacy SDK with no async version
items.why: Blocking I/O: a thread (or asyncio.to_thread) avoids freezing the loop.

items.text: Computing sales statistics in pure Python over millions of rows

items.code:
async def f():
    return 1

print(f())
options: <coroutine object f at 0x...> and a RuntimeWarning
items.why: Calling an async function creates a coroutine but doesn't run it. You need await f() or asyncio.run(f()).
